why: Commits 2 and 3 leave real choices: which readers a cold store and platform frame await ('open that file and call the same functions'), how each of 14 features is switched on through its own saver found by reading admin actions, and what to do when Postgres's per-table counters do not settle. The figures are only meaningful if the database the test meets is the same each time, and pnpm test:int runs it after every other integration file has added stores and rows, so making the counts stable is a design problem, not a fill-in.
harm_if_wrong: A budget test that wobbles or was written on a different database than CI's turns the integration job red for no reason, or one bent until it passes holds nothing; the app itself is not touched beyond commit 1.
make_it_cheaper: Name in the brief, for each of the 14 features, the exact server function and arguments that switch it on, list the layout readers of frame.store and frame.platform by name, and have the test count only statements (rows read as report-only) against a database it seeds in its own schema-free run, so commits 2 and 3 become cheap-then-review.
brief_problems: src/db/statement-count.ts does not exist yet (step 1.9 makes it); stop_if 1 covers it.

The baseline is written on a freshly seeded database, but pnpm test:int runs this file after the other integration files, which add stores, orders and pages; jobs that loop over every store or scan whole tables will count differently there, so 'the same figures three times' on a fresh database does not mean CI passes.

pg_stat_user_tables counts every backend's reads, including the dedicated reader connection's own pg_stat queries and any background work, so rowsRead may never be exactly repeatable; stop_if 4 admits this but the brief still makes rowsRead a failing figure.
The route keeps about 77 lines matching the key-count regex the check uses, which includes nested object lines, so 'count both with rg -c' may not count keys alone.
